title: Oboe reeds and Rico number twos
summary: Oboists make their own double reeds, but Holmes never learned to shave a reed, so he bought boxes of Rico number twos.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Reeds, mouthpieces and horns: the reed player's gear

blocks.x: But you know more about that, even so, because you have played oboe.
Well, oboe has nothing to do with clarinet.
No, but I mean, that has to do with resonance in the reed.
Oh yeah, yeah, the resonance, sure.
Yeah, because isn't an oboe a double reed?
Yeah, it's a double reed and very small. Very small and very hard to blow.
And that's where you have to get the vibration.
Yeah. And you're supposed to make your own reeds with the oboe. You're supposed to.

Yeah. Most oboe players, they make their own reeds. Which I never got that far with it. No, I would buy a reed and let it get soft after soaking it, and this-that-and-the-other. I never could shave a reed. I was never successful shaving any kind of a reed. Even saxophone. I never know the right place to shave a reed. I tried it for years. I could never shave a reed successfully. And then I got to using a certain brand reed, and they had them numbered, and that was...

A Number-two, you know. It's funny, I got that name. That name came to me. Rico, yeah. You see, because I haven't been playing lately... Rico. They come in numbers. So #2 satisfied me more than #2-1/2. #2-1/2 is a little bit too stiff for my mouthpiece, and with the #2 I could get the resonance that I wanted, you know.

Well, rather than me bother to shavin' reeds and cuttin' them down, I'd buy reeds by the boxes, and I didn't have no trouble. I had no trouble because the Number-Two fitted me pretty good. And I'd just put the reed on and go ahead and play it. And they lasted me quite a while. I was glad for that, because I was never successful shaving reeds. I mean, some people can do it, and do very good...
